newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crude demand thin, cost seen rising.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crude demand thin, cost seen rising.

text.p: U.S. foreign crude demand was thin Tuesday with buyers shying away from expensive imports due to a tightly shut arbitrage, traders said.
Firming crude oil prices across the Atlantic from a wave of refinery buying today also further dampened U.S. interest.
"The market has come to a screeching halt. There's just not a lot of spot cargoes nor interest," an East Coast trader said, noting sales efforts into the U.S. had fizzled.
A U.S. trader with two million barrels of Brent recently sold its second one million barrel shipment in Europe, after attempting to sell Brent at West Texas Intermediate parity.
Brent into the U.S. was pegged at WTI plus 10-20 cents, deemed uncompetitive against domestics like Light Louisiana Sweet, which traded up to plus 37 cents.
West African cargo fixtures were sighted, but traders said spot prices were difficult to discern in the thin market.
Foracados was assessed at WTI plus 70 cents cif, with Bonny Light 10-15 cents weaker for second-half Oct.
In regional trade, Chile's state firm ENAP sought to buy a million barrels of crude for Nov 6-10 delivery.
Traders said spot supplies were thin as equity sellers had signed off Argentine and Colombian supplies recently.
A U.S. trader last week secured Vasconia around WTI minus $2.00 fob, while a three-month Cano Limon contract was also heard sold at an undisclosed price.
In the aftermarket, several cargoes of Nov Brent moved between $23 to $23.05 a barrel, five to 10 cents firmer than the IPE close.
And intermonth Nov/Dec traded between 54-57 cents, nine cents higher than the London session.
